note: Draft — proposed, not sealed. The rule this file records was worked out in a chat where a Nestor triage over 37 open items from willow-mcp's backlog surfaced an 11-family cluster whose members all asked one shape of question ('should we build X now?') and shared one shape of answer ('earn-first / no consumer / wait'). The rule below is the single policy call those 11 collapse to. The mechanism that enforces it is willow-memory/willow-mcp#382, merged to master 2026-08-26. Sealing this file is the operator's; propose-not-confirm applies (CLAUDE.md, agent-guide.md).

decisions.question: What earns an earn-first tool — i.e. what moves a family out of the 'don't build ahead of a consumer' tier?
decisions.commitment: The operator asks for it AND agrees, on the record, to what the ask opens. The record is a build lease: a JSON file under mcp_apps/_build_leases/<tool>.json, keyed by tool-family name, carrying issuer + granted_at + expires_at + ttl_seconds + reason. Written by 'willow-mcp grant-build <tool> --ttl 30m --reason "..."', a local-only CLI unreachable from any MCP tool. When the lease is active the family may be built and shipped; when it expires the family falls back to earn-first and any further work needs a fresh ask under the same terms. The reason field is where the agreement lives — an empty reason still writes a lease (a re-grant to extend an in-flight session should not be blocked on rewording) but the CLI prints a NOTE flagging it, because the rule this seal opens is that the operator asks AND agrees, and an empty reason has nowhere for the agreement to live.
decisions.why: 'A consumer will earn it' was the rule the fleet already had, and it failed in a shape Nestor's triage made visible: 11 of 37 open backlog items sat in an ambiguity zone because 'consumer' had no operational definition anywhere except integrations.py (docs/design/integrations.md §6 — the 'twice, cite both' checklist over ledger citations). Every other earn-first row was re-argued case-by-case. Reframing 'consumer' as 'the operator, on the record' fixes the frame — callers don't earn authority, the person accountable for the surface does — and reusing the grant-net lease shape means no new machinery. Two fleet calls with no human on the record is exactly the failure shape B-35 documents (envelope metering with no citation writer — a counter that counts nothing); a lease with an issuer, an expiry, and a reason cannot fail that way.

decisions.question: Why the 3h ceiling, and why reuse the grant-net lease shape at all?
decisions.commitment: 3h is not new — it is FRANK cc553729, the same ceiling grant-net already enforces on open-web egress leases (lease.MAX_TTL_SECONDS = 3*60*60). Reusing the shape means one directory pattern (_net_leases/ and _build_leases/ as siblings under mcp_apps/, both covered by B-14's bound_ro sandbox mount), one fail-closed reader (absent / unparseable / naive-timestamped / over-ceiling / mismatched-subject all read as *no lease*), one mint boundary (local CLI only, blocked from MCP tools, blocked from agent Bash by the PreToolUse self-grant guard extended for grant-build in willow-mcp c474ff4), one panel row shape (timer_shape=lease, countdown when active, grant action when dry), and one place in diagnostic_summary that reports the residual. build_lease.py in willow-mcp is a parallel module of lease.py because parallel implementations of the same failure mode are safer than a shared parameterization that could drift on one axis without the other noticing.
decisions.why: The convention across the fleet — consent.py, lease.py, identity_binding.py, envelope registry — is that trust artifacts read fail-closed and mint boundaries are physical (a directory the agent's uid cannot write, backed by B-32 / WILLOW_MCP_STRICT_TRUST_ROOT). A build authorization sits in the same trust posture as a runtime authorization: same threat model, same audit trail, same decay-by-default. Inventing a second shape here would have meant a second audit surface and a second failure mode to keep in sync. The reason the ceiling isn't 24h or 'until revoked' is exactly the reason grant-net's is 3h — a standing authorization the operator forgets they granted is the shape B-32 exists to close.

decisions.question: What is the scope of this rule right now — every earn-first gate, or only the ones this decision names?
decisions.commitment: Only the ones this decision names, though the rule shape is intended for most gates over time. The concrete roster today is willow-mcp's build_lease.EARN_FIRST_ROSTER (9 families: workflow, intake, dag, tension_scan, source_trail_verify, infer, dream, wce, voice_keyterms), covering the earn-first tier in docs/design/slice-backlog.md and the operator-promoted-from-LEAVE rows (2026-07-21). Each additional gate joining the rule is its own subsequent seal — this file does not authorize adding rows to EARN_FIRST_ROSTER, and the roster's location as a module-level tuple (not a JSON file) makes 'adding a family to the gated set' a code diff a reviewer sees. Integration stubs stay on a different rule (earn_mode: two-cite, per integrations.py's earned_by field and the twice-cited ledger checklist) — different subject, different check.
decisions.why: The user's language was 'most gates, but just the ones we're talking about' — an intent about shape without a mandate about coverage. Sealing coverage inline would either overreach (rewrite every gate's earn-condition in one commit) or drift (list gates today that later turn out not to fit). Sealing the shape and leaving each gate's opt-in to its own decision matches the fleet's existing pattern for envelope-precedent extension and permission-group additions.

decisions.question: What happened to gcal and idea-timetravel, which showed up in the cluster Nestor grouped?
decisions.commitment: Both left the earn-first cluster deliberately. gcal (google-calendar OAuth transport) is misclassified as earn-first — the operator ask already exists (commitment ingestion is the citation), and the block is the OAuth flow, not an operator ask that hasn't happened. Moved to earn_mode: auth-flow-blocked in slice-backlog.md; not gated by this rule. idea-timetravel (full agent-state reconstruction from receipts + lineage) was a Nestor false-positive — the string matcher grouped it with 'should we build X?' items on skeleton overlap, but it is a debug idea, not a capability with a caller shape. Kicked out of the cluster; stays in the idea pile in willow-mcp docs/ideas.md #72 with 🟡 partial status.
decisions.why: This is worth recording because it names a class of Nestor triage output the seat should not trust blindly. The string matcher at the 0.45 bar clusters questions on shared skeleton ('Should we build X?', 'Should there be Y?'), which is real signal for some tasks (finding the 11-family cluster this decision resolves) and pure noise for others (grouping a debug idea with build proposals). The triage docstring itself flags this — the semantic matcher would close the gap where the model is reachable, but on a seat that cannot download fastembed the honest thing is to look at each cluster member and drop the ones the shared skeleton was the whole reason they grouped.
